attribution: Classic brewing-city ion concentrations (ppm) compiled from the standard homebrewing literature — Palmer & Kaminski 'Water', the Bru'n Water knowledge base, and A.J. deLange's historical analyses. Municipal water varies seasonally and with treatment; these are the historical/representative profiles brewers target, not a current tap analysis. Style-target profiles follow the Bru'n Water colour-and-balance framework.

profiles.name: Burton upon Trent
profiles.description: The most famous brewing water on earth. Enormously high sulfate from the local gypsum accentuates hop bitterness into a crisp, dry, minerally snap — the 'Burton snap' — and made the town the historic capital of pale ale. So influential that adding gypsum to liquor is still called 'Burtonisation'.

profiles.name: Dublin
profiles.description: Very high bicarbonate alkalinity — the reason Dublin became a stout city. Only heavily roasted, acidic dark malts can balance the mash pH this water pushes up, which is exactly what Guinness-style dry stout is built from.

profiles.name: Munich
profiles.description: Moderately alkaline, low in sulfate and chloride — a clean, malt-forward profile that suits amber and dark Bavarian lagers. The alkalinity is balanced by the darker malts in dunkel and bock; for pale Helles, brewers now dilute or acidify.

profiles.name: Pilsen
profiles.description: Astonishingly soft — almost distilled. This near-zero mineral content is what lets Bohemian Pilsner show its delicate Saaz hop and Pilsner malt character without any mineral interference. The template for every soft-water pale lager.

profiles.name: London
profiles.description: Moderately hard and moderately alkaline, with chloride edging out sulfate for a rounder, maltier balance — well suited to the porters, milds, and browns that defined London brewing.

profiles.name: Dortmund
profiles.description: Very hard water with substantial sulfate AND alkalinity — a high-mineral profile that gives Dortmunder Export its firm, slightly minerally, hop-balanced character distinct from softer Munich Helles.

profiles.name: Edinburgh
profiles.description: Hard, alkaline water that supported Edinburgh's malt-forward Scottish ales; the alkalinity and moderate sulfate suit rich, malty brews rather than aggressively hoppy ones.

profiles.name: Vienna
profiles.description: Hard and alkaline with moderate sulfate — a profile that shaped the amber, malty Vienna lager style.

profiles.name: Cologne (Köln)
profiles.description: Moderate hardness with chloride well above sulfate, giving Kölsch its soft, rounded, subtly malty delicacy under a crisp finish.

profiles.name: Brussels
profiles.description: Moderately hard, moderately alkaline water of the Senne valley — the historic water of lambic and Belgian wheat.

profiles.name: Tadcaster
profiles.description: A hard, sulfate-rich Yorkshire brewing town (home of Samuel Smith's and John Smith's); a gentler cousin of Burton's water for firm, dry bitters.

profiles.name: Bohemia (soft supply)
profiles.description: A representative soft Bohemian supply just above Pilsen's near-zero baseline; the template for delicate Czech pale lager.

profiles.name: Asheville, North Carolina
profiles.description: Very soft Appalachian mountain water; a blank slate that helped make Asheville a dense craft-brewing hub.

profiles.name: Bend, Oregon
profiles.description: Soft Cascade snowmelt behind Central Oregon's outsized brewery count.

profiles.name: Melbourne
profiles.description: Soft protected-catchment water supplying one of the southern hemisphere's busiest craft scenes.

profiles.name: Bamberg
profiles.description: Hard, alkaline Franconian water behind Bamberg's smoked lagers and dark Franconian styles.

profiles.name: Tokyo
profiles.description: Moderately soft municipal water supplying Japan's dense Tokyo craft scene; a light, flexible base.

profiles.name: Copenhagen
profiles.description: Hard, chalky Danish groundwater — historically the water of Carlsberg's lagers.

profiles.name: Portland, Maine
profiles.description: Very soft Sebago Lake water behind the outsized New England hazy-IPA scene (Bissell Brothers, Foundation, etc.).

profiles.name: Chico, California
profiles.description: Soft, low-mineral water — the tap water behind Sierra Nevada and a big reason clean, hop-showcasing American pale ale developed here. A near-blank canvas that brewers build up with salts to taste.

profiles.name: San Diego, California
profiles.description: Moderately hard, moderately alkaline Colorado River water with meaningful sulfate — heavily treated by the West Coast IPA breweries that made the city famous. Most SD brewers dilute with RO and rebuild toward a high-sulfate hoppy profile.

profiles.name: Portland, Oregon
profiles.description: Bull Run reservoir water is extraordinarily soft — nearly as clean as Pilsen. A blank slate the Oregon craft scene builds up for any style.

profiles.name: Denver, Colorado
profiles.description: Soft-to-moderate Rocky Mountain snowmelt; a flexible, lightly mineralised base used across Colorado's large craft scene.

profiles.name: Target: Pale & Balanced
profiles.description: A general-purpose pale-beer target: enough calcium for healthy mashing and yeast, low alkalinity for a pale grist, and even sulfate/chloride for a balanced finish.

profiles.name: Target: Pale & Hoppy
profiles.description: The modern West Coast IPA target — high sulfate (150–250 ppm) over low chloride for a crisp, dry, assertively bitter finish. Effectively a controlled Burtonisation.

profiles.name: Target: Hazy & Juicy
profiles.description: The NEIPA target: chloride pushed well above sulfate (often 2:1) for a soft, full, 'juicy' mouthfeel that rounds off hop bitterness rather than sharpening it.

profiles.name: Target: Amber & Balanced
profiles.description: A malt-leaning target for amber styles: some alkalinity to balance moderate crystal-malt acidity, with even sulfate/chloride.

profiles.name: Target: Brown & Balanced
profiles.description: For brown and dark-amber styles: enough alkalinity to offset roast acidity, chloride-forward for malt roundness.

profiles.name: Target: Black & Balanced
profiles.description: For stouts and porters: substantial alkalinity (100–200 ppm) to buffer heavy roasted malts, chloride-forward for a smooth, full body.

profiles.name: Target: Black & Roasty-Bitter
profiles.description: A Dublin-leaning dry-stout target: high alkalinity to support the roast, but sulfate over chloride to keep the finish dry and the roast bitterness crisp.

profiles.name: Reverse Osmosis / Distilled
profiles.description: Zero-ion blank slate. Many modern brewers start here and add salts precisely, rather than trying to correct an unknown or variable tap supply.
